items.title: Loic Bruni Reveals How Serious His Injury Really Was
items.description:
Loïc Bruni isn’t finished yet.

Seven years after his last appearance on the Downtime Podcast, one of the defining downhill racers of his generation joins Chris in person at a very different point in his career.

After a heavy crash in Loudenvielle brought his 2026 season to an abrupt halt, Loïc is rebuilding from one of the most serious injuries of his career. A badly dislocated wrist required urgent surgery, while questions remain around the nerve issue that may have contributed to his hand unexpectedly coming off the handlebar in the first place.

At 32, recovery feels different.

Loïc talks candidly about the dark days of being unable to race, struggling with confidence, rebuilding strength and mobility, and trying to balance rehabilitation with life as a new father.

But retirement is not the plan. Loïc still believes he can win.

We dive deep into his rivalry with Jackson Goldstone, the 2025 title battle, the redemption of finally stopping Jackson’s winning streak in Andorra, and the heartbreak of losing the overall at Mont-Sainte-Anne without getting the chance to race the final.

That rivalry still drives him.

Loïc talks about Jackson, Jordan Williams, Finn Iles and Max Alran, why he believes some of the younger riders may have more natural talent, and why he still thinks experience, preparation and work ethic can keep him at the front.

He explains how he is changing his training, bodyweight, riding position and approach to stay competitive, and why he genuinely believes he is a better racer now than he was in his twenties.

We also get into the evolution of Specialized Gravity, working alongside Nico Vouilloz, Jack Roure’s influence on his career, and what would have to happen before Loïc seriously considers retirement.

Beyond his own comeback, the conversation opens up into the wider state of downhill.

Loïc gives his thoughts on modern World Cup tracks, why predictable lines may actually be contributing to crashes and inconsistent results, how downhill could learn from Red Bull Hardline, the current broadcast, prize money, rider consultation and what the sport needs to do to attract genuinely mainstream sponsors.

After years of winning World Championships, World Cups and overall titles, Loïc Bruni has nothing left to prove.

But he still has something he wants to prove to himself.

Can Super Bruni come back and win again?

items.title: Henri Kiefer: Why Speed Isn't Enough to Win
items.description:
Henri Kiefer already knows he has the speed to compete with the fastest downhill racers in the world.

The harder challenge has been learning how to access that speed when the pressure is highest.

In this episode of the Downtime Podcast, Henri joins Chris to talk about confidence, expectation, visualisation and the mental side of racing at the very top of World Cup downhill.

We rewind to the 2025 World Championships in Champéry, where Henri arrived with an unusually strong sense of belief and produced one of the biggest rides of his career. At just 20 years old, he took Elite World Championship silver, with only Jackson Goldstone able to beat his time.

Henri explains how GoPro footage, visualisation and confidence helped him prepare, and why he believes a World Championship demands an almost extreme level of self-belief.

From there, we go back through his journey from grassroots racing in Germany and the iXS Rookies Cup to the SRAM Young Guns programme, Canyon, and his relationship with three-time World Champion Fabien Barel.

We discuss Henri's 2023 Junior World Championship victory, his move into Elite racing and the difficult transition from being one of the fastest juniors in the world to lining up against riders he'd spent years watching.

Henri also opens up about the highs and lows of his 2025 season, including mechanicals, missed qualifications, his first Elite World Cup podium, World Championship silver and a run of podium performances that suddenly made everything feel effortless.

Then came injury.

A scaphoid fracture at Mont-Sainte-Anne disrupted his off-season and contributed to a difficult start to 2026. But as Henri explains, the physical setback wasn't the whole problem.

He'd become too focused on results, comparison and what he believed he should be achieving.

Working with Fabien, his coach and his father, Henri began changing the way he approached race weekends. The shift quickly paid off with another podium at Leogang and a return to greater consistency.

Throughout the episode, we get into visualisation, routines, reflection, confidence, learning from teammates like Troy Brosnan and Luca Shaw, and the delicate balance between ambition and pressure.

Henri has already been Junior World Champion, stood on Elite World Cup podiums and finished within touching distance of an Elite rainbow jersey.

The speed isn't the question anymore.

The challenge is creating the conditions that allow that speed to appear when it matters most.
